## Purpose

This SOP provides methods for extracting, staining, and enumerating
microplastics (particles less than 5 mm) from water samples.
Microplastics are stained with Nile Red dye, vacuum-filtered onto
glass-fiber filters, and counted under fluorescence using either a
Crime-Lite forensic light source with goggles or the Echo Revolve
microscope [@maes2017; @ernicassola2017].

This SOP is intended as an internal teaching and research protocol.
Where EA Program data will be submitted to external programs or compared
with regulatory monitoring datasets, researchers should consult the
emerging standardized methods described in Appendix B and adapt
procedures accordingly [@swrcb2022; @thornton2025].


## Scope

- **Applies to:** Extraction and enumeration of microplastics from
  drinking water, surface water, stormwater, and other aqueous samples
- **Does not apply to:** Microplastics in soil, sediment, or biological
  tissue (see SCCWRP Technical Report #1410.A [@thornton2025]); chemical
  identification of polymer type (requires FTIR or Raman spectroscopy)
- **Regulatory alignment:** This SOP provides a Nile Red fluorescence
  screening method suitable for research and teaching. It does not
  replace the FTIR- or Raman-based methods required for California
  regulatory drinking water monitoring [@swrcb2022]. Consult Appendix B
  and the PI before submitting data to SWAMP, CEDEN, or other regulatory
  programs.
- **Location:** EA Program laboratory, SGM 133 and SGM 134

## Definitions

- **FTIR (Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy):** An analytical
  technique that identifies polymer type by comparing a sample's
  infrared absorption spectrum to reference spectra; the gold standard
  for confirmatory microplastic characterization [@swrcb2022].
- **Microplastic (MP):** A synthetic polymer particle or fiber with at
  least one dimension between 1 µm and 5 mm; includes fragments,
  fibers, films, beads, and foam; classified as primary (manufactured
  at micro-scale) or secondary (degradation products of larger plastic
  items) [@maes2017].
- **Nanoplastic:** A plastic particle smaller than 1 µm; not
  quantifiable by standard visual methods; an emerging concern for
  ecological and human health research.
- **Nile Red:** A fluorescent dye that selectively stains hydrophobic
  plastic surfaces, enabling detection under blue-light excitation;
  used as a screening tool to distinguish plastic particles from
  organic debris [@ernicassola2017; @maes2017].
- **Procedural blank:** A sample of laboratory-grade water carried
  through the complete analytical procedure alongside field samples;
  used to quantify airborne and procedural contamination; required for
  every analytical batch.
- **Raman spectroscopy:** A spectroscopic technique that identifies
  molecular composition from inelastic light scattering; complementary
  to FTIR; particularly useful for particles smaller than 10 µm
  [@swrcb2022].
- **Visual sorting:** The initial enumeration step in which particles
  on a filter are examined under a stereomicroscope or the Revolve
  fluorescence microscope and candidate plastic particles are
  identified by color, shape, and texture before any confirmatory
  chemical analysis.


## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Chemical:** Acetone is flammable (flash point -20 °C) and
  potentially toxic by inhalation. All Nile Red solution preparation
  and sample staining must be performed in a fume hood. Review the SDS
  for acetone before use.
- **Optical:** The Crime-Lite 2BG2735 is a high-intensity 450--510 nm
  light source. Never shine it into anyone's eyes. Always wear the
  orange filter goggles when the Crime-Lite is on.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses
- [ ] Laboratory coat (cotton preferred -- minimize synthetic fibers)
- [ ] Nitrile gloves
- [ ] Orange filter goggles (Crime-Lite enumeration only)

### Emergency Procedures

For acetone spills, extinguish all ignition sources, ventilate the
area, and clean up per
[SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling](SOP-L003-hazardous-materials-handling.qmd).
For skin or eye contact, flush with water for at least 15 minutes.

### Glassware Decontamination
A standard protocol for removing residual micro- and nanoplastics from
glassware before use has not yet been finalized. This is a critical gap
that must be addressed before results can be considered quantitative
(see Appendix A).
:::


## Reagent Preparation

### Nile Red Stock Solution

1. Working in a fume hood, dissolve Nile Red in acetone to 1 mg/mL.
2. Store in a dark amber glass bottle at room temperature.
3. Label with concentration, date, and analyst.

### Working Concentration

The working concentration is 10 µg/mL, achieved by a 100:1 dilution of
the stock. For a 500 mL water sample, add 0.5 mL of the 1 mg/mL stock
solution [@maes2017].


## Estimated Time

| Task                                   | Time                         |
|:---------------------------------------|:-----------------------------|
| Nile Red staining and incubation       | 30 minutes                   |
| Vacuum filtration (per sample)         | 10--15 minutes               |
| Filter drying (oven at 60 °C)          | 10 minutes                   |
| Enumeration (per sample, 3--10 fields) | 30--60 minutes               |
| Total per sample (excluding wait times) | Approximately 90--150 minutes |


## Procedure

### Sample Preparation and Staining

1. Minimize synthetic fiber contamination: wear a cotton lab coat, keep
   samples covered, and work in a clean area.
2. Prepare samples in 500 mL volumes in glass bottles.
3. Working in a fume hood, inject the appropriate volume of Nile Red
   stock solution (e.g., 0.5 mL for a 500 mL sample) to achieve
   10 µg/mL. Cap immediately [@maes2017].
4. Incubate with the injected dye for at least 30 minutes at room
   temperature.

### Vacuum Filtration

5. Place a Whatman 934-AH glass-fiber filter (42.5 mm, 1.5 µm pore)
   on the fritted base of the vacuum filtration apparatus.
6. Vacuum-filter each sample through the filter.
7. Dry the filter on a watch glass in the oven at 60 °C for 10 minutes.

### Enumeration Option A: Crime-Lite with Goggles

::: {.callout-warning}
### Laser Safety
Do not shine the Crime-Lite into anyone's eyes. Never observe
illuminated samples without the orange filter goggles.
:::

8. Place the dried filter on a dark, non-reflective surface.
9. Put on the orange filter goggles.
10. Illuminate the filter with the Crime-Lite (450--510 nm).
11. Count fluorescing particles through the goggles, or mount the
    filter under the dissecting scope with a 550 nm emission filter.
12. Record particle counts and morphology (fiber, fragment, bead, film).

### Enumeration Option B: Echo Revolve Microscope (Fluorescence)

13. Mount the dried filter on a glass slide per
    [SOP-L211](SOP-L211-revolve-microscope.qmd).
14. Use the fluorescence channel (excitation ~470 nm, emission
    ~550 nm long-pass).
15. Photograph and count fluorescent particles in at least 3 randomly
    selected fields of view.
16. Import images into the Revolve app; use the annotation tools to
    mark and count particles.


## Quality Control

- Include at least one procedural blank per analytical batch; blank
  particle counts inform the detection threshold for field samples
  [@maes2017; @ernicassola2017].
- Analyze at least 3 (preferably 10) randomly selected fields of view
  per filter; report mean, standard deviation, and coefficient of
  variation.
- Include at least one spiked filter (known number of plastic particles
  added before staining) per batch to verify Nile Red staining
  performance.

::: {.callout-important}
### Contamination Controls Are Essential
Every batch must include procedural blanks processed identically to
samples. Without blanks, microplastic counts cannot be meaningfully
interpreted [@maes2017].
:::


## Troubleshooting

| Problem                          | Probable Cause                    | Corrective Action                     |
|:---------------------------------|:----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|
| High blank counts                | Airborne contamination; dirty glassware | Improve lab cleanliness; decontaminate glassware |
| No fluorescence on spiked samples | Nile Red concentration too low; degraded dye | Verify stock; prepare fresh solution |
| Fluorescence fades during counting | Photobleaching                  | Minimize illumination time; work quickly |
| Organic matter fluoresces        | Nile Red binding to natural organics | Consider H~2~O~2~ digestion pre-treatment |


## Waste Disposal

| Waste Type                       | Disposal Method                          |
|:---------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Acetone waste (Nile Red solution) | Collect in halogenated/organic waste; EH&S pickup |
| Used glass-fiber filters         | Standard trash                           |
| Sample water (post-filtration)   | Drain to sink                            |

## Training Record

Before performing microplastics analysis independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Complete [SOP-L002](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd) and
   [SOP-L003](SOP-L003-hazardous-materials-handling.qmd) training
3. Review the SDS for acetone and Nile Red
4. Complete [SOP-L211 Revolve Microscope](SOP-L211-revolve-microscope.qmd)
   training (if using the Revolve for enumeration)
5. Demonstrate safe Crime-Lite operation under supervision
6. Process at least one procedural blank and one spiked sample under
   supervision with acceptable results
7. Be signed off by the PI or lab manager

## Appendix B: Regulatory and Standards Context {.appendix}

In 2022, the California State Water Resources Control Board approved a
policy requiring drinking water agencies to monitor microplastics,
specifying FTIR and Raman spectroscopy as the two approved analytical
methods [@swrcb2022]. Standardized collection procedures for aquatic
biota and sediment are described in SCCWRP Technical Report #1410.A
[@thornton2025].

The Nile Red fluorescence screening method in this SOP is appropriate
for teaching and exploratory research but does not meet California
regulatory requirements [@swrcb2022]. For data intended for submission
to SWAMP or CEDEN:

1. Use microplastics-analysis-grade water for all blanks and rinses
2. Adopt SCCWRP contamination control procedures
3. Confirm polymer identity on a subset of particles by FTIR or Raman
4. Consult the PI before beginning any study intended for regulatory
   submission
